newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-House of Fraser set for H1 loss.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-House of Fraser set for H1 loss.

text.p: House of Fraser Plc is set to stay in the red when it reports first half results on Tuesday, but investors are likely to pay more attention to new management's efforts to revive the department store chain.
The retailer is forecast to turn in a pretax loss of between 3.0 and 7.0 million stg, against a loss of 4.3 million last year. The dividend is set to stay at 1.7 pence a share.

The group, with 51 stores around Britain, has been beset by difficulties since its flotation in 1994. It has struggled to overcome problems with store sites, stock management and cost structures, analysts said.
It was tipped as a bid target earlier this year and newspapers at the time pointed to Sears Plc, whose flagship is Selfridges department store, as a potential predator.

Its disappointing performance prompted a top management shake-up earlier this year, when chief executive Andrew Jennings was replaced by John Coleman, previously managing director of Texas Homecare, the home decor business which J. Sainsbury Plc bought from Ladbroke Plc in 1995.

Analysts said there was some scepticism about his ability to turn the business around when his appointment was announced. It could be too early to judge what impact he has made as his new management team would not have had time to make their mark.

The group is still in the process of refurbishing its stores. A brand new House of Fraser store opened in Swindon in south west England earlier this month and a refurbished store in Leeds in northern England is due to open next week.
Gross margins are likely to have come under pressure as the group has been clearing stocks of own label womenswear, which did not sell well, analysts said.

But Britain's retail revival will have helped sales, analysts said. They pointed to rival department store John Lewis, which has seen sales storm ahead over the summer and Allders Plc which has been doing well in household durables because of the housing market upturn. -- Jane Merriman, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
